opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a bit of a paradox people notice here. The things we humans consider the hardest, like competition math, advanced physics problems, or difficult coding challenges, are turning out to be among the first things AI gets really good at. Meanwhile, things a child can do, like tidying a room, or handling a messy, open-ended task over several days, are still surprisingly hard.

My explanation is that "intellectually challenging for humans" and "hard for AI" are measuring different things. For humans, math or physics is hard because our brains didn't evolve for it. We have limited working memory, we get tired, and it takes years of training to build the right intuitions. But from a learning perspective, these domains are actually very clean. The rules are well defined, the problems are self-contained, and most importantly the answers can be verified. You can check whether a proof is correct or whether code passes the tests.

That verifiability matters a lot for how current models are trained. With reinforcement learning, if you have a reliable signal of right and wrong, the model can try many times, get feedback, and improve. Math and coding are almost ideal environments for that. There's also an enormous amount of high-quality written material in these fields. People have spent centuries writing down their reasoning very explicitly, so the pretraining data already contains a lot of the structure.

Compare that with work most people consider easy but which actually depends on a huge amount of implicit context: knowing what your colleague really meant, what matters to your boss, how to prioritize when goals are vague, how to keep going on a task that lasts weeks without clear feedback. That knowledge is rarely written down, and success is hard to define. So there's no clean reward signal.

So I'd say AI isn't good at "the hardest" things in some absolute sense. It's good at things that are well specified, verifiable, and richly documented, which happen to overlap with what we label elite intellectual work. The real frontier now is moving from those clean, closed problems toward open-ended, long-horizon tasks in the real world, where the challenge is less about raw reasoning and more about context, judgment, and defining what "good" even means.

r001.rationale: The response says AI performs well on tasks with clear rules and verifiable answers, conveying that more objectively assessable tasks are easier for AI.

r002.rationale: It explains that reliable right-or-wrong feedback lets models improve through reinforcement learning, directly linking evaluation to how AI can be trained.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the surprise comes from a wrong intuition about what "hard" means. Humans equate difficulty with the work only a few people can do: math olympiad problems, writing proofs, competitive programming. But that kind of difficulty is partly an artifact of our own limitations. It takes humans years of training because our working memory is tiny and we forget. For a model, those tasks are actually the friendliest environment possible: the problem is fully specified in text, the reasoning stays inside symbols, and there is a clear signal for whether you got it right. That last point is the key. Reinforcement learning works when you can verify. Math and code are verifiable, so you can let the model try millions of times, keep what works, and it gets genuinely better. That is roughly how o1 and later reasoning models came about.

Meanwhile the things we consider easy, like driving across a city or cleaning a kitchen, are hard precisely because the reward is messy, the environment is noisy, and there is no cheap simulator. So the ranking of difficulty for AI is almost inverted from the human ranking. It is Moravec's paradox, just showing up again at a higher level.

I'd add one more thing. Pretraining gave the models an enormous prior over human reasoning, basically all the ways people have written down their thinking. What was missing was the ability to use that prior in a loop: think, act, observe, adjust. Once you add that agentic structure and train on outcomes, the "most intellectually challenging" tasks turn out to be the first dominoes to fall, not the last.

r001.rationale: The response says tasks with fully specified inputs, symbolic reasoning, and clear correctness signals are especially friendly for AI, and contrasts them with messy tasks. This conveys that more objective, verifiable tasks are easier for AI.

r002.rationale: It identifies verification as the key to reinforcement learning: math and code are verifiable, so models can be trained through repeated attempts and successful outcomes.

astra-6.text:
I think we often confuse what is difficult for humans with what is difficult for machines. We call mathematics or programming intellectually challenging because people need years of training to do them well. But those tasks also have structure: you can describe a problem precisely, and often you can check whether an answer is correct. That makes them relatively suitable for AI.

By contrast, something that feels ordinary to us—navigating an unfamiliar environment, understanding what someone actually wants, or handling an unexpected situation—can be very difficult for a machine. Humans bring a lot of experience to those tasks without even noticing it.

So I wouldn’t interpret AI’s performance on a hard intellectual task as evidence that it can automatically do everything easier than that. Difficulty isn’t a single ladder. A system might solve a sophisticated programming problem and still struggle to figure out which problem is worth solving. For work, that distinction matters: producing an answer is one part; identifying the goal, dealing with ambiguity, and making sure the result actually helps are other parts.

r001.rationale: The response says tasks with precise structure and checkable answers are relatively suitable for AI, conveying that more objective, verifiable work is easier for AI to do well at.

r002.rationale: It mentions checking whether an answer is correct, but does not say that figuring out how to evaluate a task reveals how to train AI for it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to distinguish between what feels intellectually challenging to humans and what is difficult for a machine to learn. Those aren’t necessarily the same thing.

Take mathematics or programming. They require a lot of training for a person, so we regard them as highly intellectual. But they also have relatively clear rules, and often you can check whether an answer is correct. That gives an AI a useful learning signal. By contrast, a task that seems ordinary—handling an ambiguous request, recognizing that you’re missing some information, or coordinating with people—can be much harder to specify and evaluate.

So I wouldn’t interpret AI’s performance as evidence that intellectual work is somehow easy. It tells us that our human ranking of difficulty is shaped by our own capabilities and limitations. A system can be very strong at solving a well-defined problem and still struggle to figure out which problem needs solving.

r001.rationale: The response says tasks with clear rules and checkable answers give AI a useful learning signal, while ambiguous tasks are harder to specify and evaluate. This conveys that more objective tasks are easier for AI to handle well.

r002.rationale: It links being able to check whether an answer is correct with a useful learning signal, and says harder-to-evaluate tasks are harder to specify. This communicates that evaluation structure informs how AI can be trained.
